subject: science
topic: The common belief that 'multitasking' is a real human cognitive ability
angle: The brain incurs a measurable cognitive cost when switching between tasks or strategies, though this cost can be mitigated by sequence-level processes or strategy appropriateness.
title: The Cost of Switching

hooks.text: Can your brain actually do two things at once?
You think you are multitasking. Your brain sees a sequence of costs.
You are paying a cognitive tax on every notification.
A cursor blinks on a blank screen.
Task switching has a measurable cost.

reveal.headline: Your brain pays a physical cost to switch tasks.
reveal.body: The evidence shows that switching between different cognitive strategies or tasks causes measurable delays in your response times and alters your neural connectivity.

explain.headline: Switching is not seamless.
explain.body: When you move between tasks, your brain incurs a cost in time and neural activity. This cost decreases only when a strategy becomes more appropriate for the problem you are solving.

matters.headline: Your focus is being taxed.
matters.body: That may be why you feel drained. Your brain is not multitasking; it is constantly paying a fee to reset its internal control structure every time you shift your attention.

example.headline: A quiet afternoon at your desk.
example.body: You type a sentence, glance at a notification, and then try to remember where you left off in your paragraph. You feel a momentary lag in your thinking.

question.headline: How much of your day is spent paying this tax?

claims.text: There is no switch cost at the first serial position across sequences, which is the point where sequence-level processes are likely active in maintaining or instantiating a hierarchical control structure in working memory.
claims.quote: recurrent finding of no switch cost at the first serial position across sequences, the point at which sequence-level processes are likely active in maintaining or instantiating a hierarchical control structure in working memory.

claims.text: Switch cost is negatively correlated with a set of iFC involved ROIs including left inferior frontal junction, bilateral superior posterior parietal cortex, left precuneus, bilateral inferior parietal lobule, right middle frontal gyrus and bilateral middle occipital gyrus.
claims.quote: This analysis found that switch cost was negatively correlated with a set of iFC involved ROIs including left inferior frontal junction, bilateral superior posterior parietal cortex, left precuneus, bilateral inferior parietal lobule, right middle frontal gyrus and bilateral middle occipital gyrus.

claims.text: Switching between two different cognitive strategies for a numerosity judgement task causes longer response times on switch trials compared to non-switch trials.
claims.quote: Both experiments revealed that switching between strategies entailed a cognitive cost that was reflected in longer response times on switch compared to non-switch trials but not in reduced accuracy.

claims.text: Pain, fatigue and excessive interoceptive monitoring are linked to a decrease in externally directed attention, which increases susceptibility to distraction and slows information processing in multitasking.
claims.quote: We hypothesise that pain, fatigue and excessive interoceptive monitoring produce a decrease in externally directed attention. This increases susceptibility to distraction and slows information processing, interfering with cognitive function, in particular multitasking.

claims.text: The size of the switch cost between strategies tends to diminish as a strategy becomes more appropriate for solving a particular problem.
claims.quote: The size of this switch cost did not differ as a function of strategy complexity but tended to diminish as a strategy became more appropriate for solving a particular problem.

verdict: The evidence confirms that task-switching involves a measurable cognitive cost in terms of time and neural connectivity, rather than seamless multitasking.
caveat: The sources focus primarily on the mechanics of switching and preparation rather than providing a direct measurement of overall 'intelligence' degradation.
caption:
Multitasking is a myth of efficiency. 

Research shows that switching between tasks or strategies creates a measurable cognitive cost in time and neural connectivity. While this cost can be mitigated by sequence-level processes or strategy appropriateness, it is not a seamless transition. These findings do not directly measure overall intelligence degradation.
